title: The purpose of quality management
blurb: Outline what quality management is for, and name its four parts: planning, assurance, control and continuous improvement.
question: A sponsor asks why a GP surgery refurbishment needs 'quality management' at all, when the contractor will simply inspect each room at the end. How should the project manager explain the purpose of quality management?

teach.h: Building quality in, not just checking at the end
teach.body: Quality management is the discipline for ensuring that the outputs, the benefits and the processes by which they are delivered meet stakeholder requirements and are fit for purpose. In plain English: it is the whole organised effort to get quality right, from agreeing what 'good' looks like, through checking the way work is done, to testing what is produced and learning for next time. It runs throughout the project, not just at the end.

teach.h: The four parts of quality management
teach.caption: Learn all four by name. Continuous improvement is the one candidates most often forget.

head: Part
What it does
Focus
rows: Sets acceptance criteria, standards and methods
Gives confidence the agreed processes are followed
Inspects, measures and tests the outputs
Uses lessons to improve the way work is done

teach.h: The purpose: why it is worth doing
teach.body: Quality management exists to deliver outputs that are fit for purpose and meet stakeholder requirements. Done well, it brings fewer defects and less rework (problems are prevented or caught early, when they are cheaper to fix), stakeholder confidence and satisfaction (people can see quality is under control), and compliance with the relevant standards, regulations and contracts.

steps.label:
Assure the
process
steps.sub: Check the agreed way is followed

teach.body: Harbourside GP Surgery is refurbishing six consulting rooms. Quality planning sets the acceptance criteria (infection-control finishes, sink positions, lighting levels). The practice's PMO checks the contractor follows its agreed installation procedures (assurance). Each room is inspected and tested against the criteria before sign-off (control). Snags from rooms 1 and 2 change how rooms 3 to 6 are fitted (continuous improvement). Result: fewer defects, less rework and a compliant surgery the staff trust.

teach.text: Quality management is NOT the same as quality control. Control (inspecting and testing outputs) is only one of four parts. Watch also for distractor lists that belong to other topics: 'identification, analysis and response' is risk management, and 'request, evaluation, decision' is change control.

teach.h: Quality management across a linear life cycle

items.label: Expectations captured
items.sub: Quality needs noted in the outline case

items.label: Assurance and control
items.sub: Processes assured, outputs inspected and tested

items.label: Acceptance and learning
items.sub: Outputs accepted, lessons fed into improvement

teach.caption: Illustrative: quality management is active in every phase, not bolted on at the end.

items: Quality management: the discipline for ensuring outputs, benefits and the processes that deliver them meet stakeholder requirements and are fit for purpose.
Four parts: quality planning, quality assurance, quality control and continuous improvement.
Purpose: fit-for-purpose outputs, fewer defects and less rework, stakeholder confidence and satisfaction, compliance.
It runs throughout the life cycle. It is much more than inspecting at the end.

summary: You can now outline the purpose of quality management: fit-for-purpose outputs, fewer defects and less rework, stakeholder confidence and compliance. You can also name its four parts and explain why it beats inspection at the end alone.

A.q: Which of the following best describes quality management on a project?
options: Inspecting the finished outputs to find any defects
Ensuring outputs and processes meet requirements
Identifying, analysing and responding to risks
Controlling changes to the approved baseline
A.why: Quality management is the discipline for ensuring outputs, benefits and the processes that deliver them meet stakeholder requirements and are fit for purpose.

whyNot.0: Inspecting outputs is quality control, just one of the four parts of quality management.
whyNot.2: Identifying, analysing and responding to risks describes risk management.
whyNot.3: Controlling changes to the baseline is change control.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the parts that make up quality management?
A.why: The four parts are quality planning, quality assurance, quality control and continuous improvement. A configuration audit belongs to configuration management.

whyNot.0: Quality planning is one of the four parts: it sets the criteria and standards.
whyNot.1: Quality assurance is one of the four parts: it gives confidence processes are followed.
whyNot.3: Continuous improvement is one of the four parts: it uses lessons to improve processes.

A.q: What is a key purpose of quality management?
options: To reduce defects and avoidable rework
To fix the scope so it cannot change
To make the sponsor carry out testing
To remove the need for a business case
A.why: By planning quality in and checking processes and outputs, quality management prevents or catches defects early, reducing rework.

whyNot.1: Scope is controlled through scope management and change control, not frozen by quality management.
whyNot.2: Testing is done by the team or inspectors; the sponsor does not carry it out.
whyNot.3: The business case justifies the project; quality management does not replace it.

B.q: Complete the statement: quality management is made up of quality planning, quality assurance, quality control and ______.
B.why: The fourth part is continuous improvement: using lessons and findings to improve the way work is done.

whyNot.0: Risk management planning belongs to risk management, a separate discipline.
whyNot.2: Change control manages changes to the baseline; it is part of scope management.
whyNot.3: Benefits realisation is part of benefits management, usually after handover.

B.q: A sponsor asks why the project needs quality management when the team will test everything at the end. Which is the best reply?
options: It removes the need for any testing
It guarantees the schedule is met
It passes quality risk to suppliers
It builds quality in from the start
B.why: Quality management plans, assures and controls quality throughout, so defects are prevented or caught early rather than discovered late.

whyNot.0: Testing (quality control) is still needed; it is one of the four parts.
whyNot.1: Quality management supports good delivery but guarantees nothing about the schedule.
whyNot.2: Quality cannot simply be handed to suppliers; the project still manages it.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are purposes of quality management?
1. Giving stakeholders confidence in the outputs
2. Guaranteeing that no risks occur
3. Helping outputs comply with relevant standards
4. Fixing the budget so it never changes
B.why: Stakeholder confidence and compliance are both purposes of quality management.

whyNot.1: Statement 4 is wrong: quality management does not freeze the budget.
whyNot.2: Statement 2 is wrong: no discipline can guarantee that no risks occur.
whyNot.3: Both statements are wrong: neither is a purpose of quality management.

C.q: On a hospital refurbishment, standards are agreed up front, a reviewer checks procedures are followed, each room is inspected before sign-off, and lessons feed into the next phase. What do these activities make up together?
C.why: Planning, assurance, control and continuous improvement together make up quality management.

whyNot.0: Risk management deals with uncertain events, not standards, inspection and process checks.
whyNot.1: Change control evaluates and decides on requests to change the baseline.
whyNot.2: Configuration management controls and records versions of configuration items.

C.q: Quality management aims to ensure that which of the following meet stakeholder requirements?
options: Only the final outputs at handover
Only the processes used by the team
Only the costs and timescales agreed
C.why: The definition covers the outputs, the benefits and the processes by which they are delivered.

whyNot.0: Outputs matter, but so do the processes and the benefits, and not only at handover.
whyNot.1: Processes matter, but quality management also covers the outputs and benefits.
whyNot.3: Cost and time are separate constraints, not what quality management ensures.

C.q: A project skipped quality management to save time. Late testing finds many defects and the client loses trust. Which purpose of quality management would most directly have helped?
C.why: Quality management prevents or catches defects early, cutting rework and keeping stakeholder confidence.

whyNot.0: The critical path concerns schedule duration, not defects.
whyNot.2: Fixing scope is about change control; it would not have prevented the defects.
whyNot.3: Releasing resources happens at closure and would not have reduced defects.

reteach.title: Think of a busy restaurant kitchen
reteach.question: A good restaurant serves consistently excellent food night after night. Tasting each plate at the end is only part of how it does that. What are the other parts?

blocks.h: Four habits of a great kitchen
blocks.body: First the recipes and presentation standards are written down (planning). The head chef watches that cooks follow the agreed methods and hygiene rules (assurance). Every plate is checked at the pass before it goes out (control). After service, complaints and wasted dishes are reviewed and recipes are tweaked (continuous improvement). Together this is quality management. Tasting at the pass alone would catch bad plates but not stop them being cooked.

blocks.text: Checking the plates (quality control) is only one part. Quality management is all four parts working together.

explain.body: Quality management is the discipline for ensuring outputs, benefits and the processes that deliver them meet stakeholder requirements and are fit for purpose.

explain.caption: All three must meet stakeholder requirements and be fit for purpose.

test.q: Quality management is best described as a discipline for ensuring what?
options: Every risk is removed before deployment
Outputs and processes are fit for purpose
test.why: Quality management ensures outputs, benefits and processes meet stakeholder requirements and are fit for purpose.

whyNot.0: Finishing early is a schedule matter, not the aim of quality management.
whyNot.1: Risks are managed, not removed, and that is risk management's job.
whyNot.2: Quality responsibility cannot simply be transferred to suppliers.

explain.body: Quality planning sets the criteria and standards. Quality assurance gives confidence processes are followed. Quality control inspects and tests outputs. Continuous improvement uses lessons to make processes better.

test.q: A team uses lessons from defects found in phase one to refine its build procedure for phase two. Which part of quality management is this?
test.why: Using lessons to improve the way work is done is continuous improvement.

whyNot.0: Quality planning sets criteria and standards before the work, not refinements from lessons.
whyNot.1: Quality control inspects and tests outputs; it found the defects but did not change the procedure.
whyNot.3: Assurance checks that agreed processes are followed; it does not itself redesign them from lessons.

explain.body: Why do it? Fit-for-purpose outputs, fewer defects and less rework, stakeholder confidence and satisfaction, and compliance with standards and regulations.

test.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of quality management?
test.why: Quality management does not guarantee early delivery; its purposes are fit-for-purpose outputs, fewer defects, confidence and compliance.

whyNot.0: Fit-for-purpose outputs are the central purpose of quality management.
whyNot.1: Fewer defects and less rework are a direct purpose of quality management.
whyNot.3: Building stakeholder confidence and satisfaction is a purpose of quality management.

explain.h: Throughout, not just at the end
explain.body: Quality management is active in every phase: planning before the work, assurance and control during it, and improvement as lessons emerge. Inspection at the end alone finds defects late, when they cost most to fix.

test.q: When should quality management activities take place on a project?
options: Only once the outputs are complete
Only if the client reports a defect
test.why: Quality management is applied throughout the life cycle, from planning through delivery to handover.

whyNot.1: Waiting until outputs are complete means defects are found late and cost more to fix.
whyNot.2: Quality management is proactive, not triggered only by complaints.
whyNot.3: Concept is too early to do it all: assurance and control happen during delivery.
